**Jennifer Joanna Aniston** (born February 11, 1969) is an American actress. Her accolades include a [Primetime Emmy Award](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award "Primetime Emmy Award"), a [Golden Globe Award](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award"), and two [Screen Actors Guild Awards](/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild_Awards "Screen Actors Guild Awards"). Aniston has consistently ranked among the world's highest-paid actresses, as of 2023.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The daughter of actors [John Aniston](/wiki/John_Aniston "John Aniston") and [Nancy Dow](/wiki/Nancy_Dow "Nancy Dow"), she began working as an actress at an early age with an uncredited role in the 1988 film *[Mac and Me](/wiki/Mac_and_Me "Mac and Me")*. Her first major film role came in the 1993 horror comedy *[Leprechaun](/wiki/Leprechaun_(film) "Leprechaun (film)")*. She rose to international fame for her role as [Rachel Green](/wiki/Rachel_Green "Rachel Green") on the television [sitcom](/wiki/Sitcom "Sitcom") *[Friends](/wiki/Friends "Friends")* from 1994 to 2004, for which she received the [Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Lead_Actress_in_a_Comedy_Series "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series").

Tharman was born in [Singapore during British colonial rule](/wiki/Colony_of_Singapore "Colony of Singapore") in 1957 to a family of [Sri Lankan Tamil](/wiki/Sri_Lankan_Tamils "Sri Lankan Tamils") origin.[[10]](#cite_note-11) In his youth, Tharman attended the [Anglo-Chinese School](/wiki/Anglo-Chinese_School "Anglo-Chinese School")[[11]](#cite_note-12) before graduating from the [London School of Economics](/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") (LSE) with a [Bachelor of Science](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in economics.

He subsequently went on to the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), where he completed a [Master of Philosophy](/wiki/Master_of_Philosophy "Master of Philosophy") degree in economics.[[12]](#cite_note-13) He then became a student at the [Harvard Kennedy School](/wiki/Harvard_Kennedy_School "Harvard Kennedy School") at [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), where he completed a [Master in Public Administration](/wiki/Master_in_Public_Administration "Master in Public Administration") (MPA) degree and was a recipient of the [Lucius N. Littauer](/wiki/Lucius_N._Littauer "Lucius N. Littauer") Fellows Award (given to MPA students who demonstrate academic excellence and leadership).

In 2011, LSE awarded him an [Honorary Fellowship](/wiki/Honorary_title_(academic) "Honorary title (academic)").[[13]](#cite_note-14)

Tharman was a [student activist](/wiki/Student_activist "Student activist") while studying in the United Kingdom during the 1970s.[[14]](#cite_note-CHL-15) He originally held [socialist](/wiki/Socialism "Socialism") beliefs, but his views on economics evolved over the course of his working career.[[14]](#cite_note-CHL-15)

Main article: [Wildlife of the United Arab Emirates](/wiki/Wildlife_of_the_United_Arab_Emirates "Wildlife of the United Arab Emirates")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/1501200713074_Acacia_tortilis.jpg/250px-1501200713074_Acacia_tortilis.jpg)](/wiki/File:1501200713074_Acacia_tortilis.jpg)

[Acacia](/wiki/Acacia "Acacia") trees growing in desert suburbs near [Fujairah](/wiki/Fujairah "Fujairah")

The UAE contains the following terrestrial ecoregions: [Al Hajar montane woodlands](/wiki/Al_Hajar_montane_woodlands "Al Hajar montane woodlands") and shrublands, [Gulf of Oman desert and semi-desert](/wiki/Gulf_of_Oman_desert_and_semi-desert "Gulf of Oman desert and semi-desert"), and Al-Hajar foothill [xeric woodlands and shrublands](/wiki/Deserts_and_xeric_shrublands "Deserts and xeric shrublands").[[106]](#cite_note-DinersteinOlson2017-109)

The oases grow [date palms](/wiki/Phoenix_dactylifera "Phoenix dactylifera"), [acacia](/wiki/Acacia "Acacia"), and [eucalyptus](/wiki/Eucalyptus "Eucalyptus") trees. In the desert, the flora is very sparse and consists of [grasses](/wiki/Grasses "Grasses") and thorn bushes. The indigenous fauna had come close to extinction because of intensive hunting, which has led to a conservation program on [Sir Bani Yas](/wiki/Sir_Bani_Yas "Sir Bani Yas") Island initiated by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in the 1970s, resulting in the survival of, for example, [Arabian Oryx](/wiki/Arabian_Oryx "Arabian Oryx"), [Arabian camel](/wiki/Arabian_camel "Arabian camel"), and [leopards](/wiki/Leopard "Leopard"). [Coastal fish](/wiki/Coastal_fish "Coastal fish") and [mammals](/wiki/Mammals "Mammals") consist mainly of [mackerel](/wiki/Mackerel "Mackerel"), [perch](/wiki/Estuary_perch "Estuary perch"), and [tuna](/wiki/Tuna "Tuna"), as well as [sharks](/wiki/Shark "Shark") and whales.

While debate as to whether the Amazon or the [Nile](/wiki/Nile "Nile") is the world's longest river has gone on for many years, the historic consensus of geographic authorities has been to regard the Amazon as the second longest river in the world, with the Nile being the longest. However, the Amazon has been reported as being anywhere between 6,275 km (3,899 mi) and 6,992 km (4,345 mi) long.[[6]](#cite_note-liu-etal-river-length-6) It is often said to be "at least" 6,400 km (4,000 mi) long.[[5]](#cite_note-britannica-amazon-5) The Nile is reported to be anywhere from 5,499 to 7,088 km (3,417 to 4,404 mi).[[6]](#cite_note-liu-etal-river-length-6) Often it is said to be "about" 6,650 km (4,130 mi) long.[[24]](#cite_note-britannica-nile-27) There are several factors that can affect these measurements, such as the position of the geographical source and the mouth, the scale of measurement, and the length measuring techniques (for details see also [List of rivers by length](/wiki/List_of_rivers_by_length "List of rivers by length")).[[6]](#cite_note-liu-etal-river-length-6)[[7]](#cite_note-river-source-7)

In July 2008, the [Brazilian Institute for Space Research (INPE)](/wiki/National_Institute_for_Space_Research "National Institute for Space Research") published a news article on their webpage, claiming that the Amazon River was 140 km (87 mi) longer than the Nile. The Amazon's length was calculated as 6,992 km (4,345 mi), taking the Apacheta Creek as its source. Using the same techniques, the length of the Nile was calculated as 6,853 km (4,258 mi), which is longer than previous estimates but still shorter than the Amazon. Yellowstone's climate is greatly influenced by altitude, with lower elevations generally found to be warmer year-round. The record high temperature was 99 °F (37 °C) in 2002, while the coldest temperature recorded is −66 °F (−54 °C) in 1933.[[11]](#cite_note-facts-11) During the summer months of June to early September, daytime highs are normally in the 70 to 80 °F (21 to 27 °C) range, while nighttime lows can go to below freezing (0 °C), especially at higher altitudes. Summer afternoons are frequently accompanied by [thunderstorms](/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm"). Spring and fall temperatures range between 30 and 60 °F (−1 and 16 °C) with nights in the teens to single digits (−5 to −20 °C). Winter in Yellowstone is accompanied by high temperatures usually between 0 and 20 °F (−18 and −7 °C) and nighttime temperatures below 0 °F (−18 °C) for most of the winter.[[145]](#cite_note-weather-148)

Precipitation in Yellowstone is highly variable and ranges from 15 inches (380 mm) annually near Mammoth Hot Springs to 80 inches (2,000 mm) in the southwestern sections of the park. The precipitation of Yellowstone is greatly influenced by the moisture channel formed by the [Snake River Plain](/wiki/Snake_River_Plain "Snake River Plain") to the west that was, in turn, formed by Yellowstone itself. Snow is possible in any month of the year, but most common between November and April, with averages of 150 inches (3,800 mm) annually around Yellowstone Lake, to twice that amount at higher elevations.[[145]](#cite_note-weather-148)

Reception to generation III's Pokémon has been polarized. Alex Carlson of *Hardcore Gamer* wrote in 2014 that the third generation of *Pokémon* games was not well received by fans of the series, with some people calling the generation the "worst in the series history".[[5]](#cite_note-HardcoreGamer-5) This was in part because *Ruby* and *Sapphire* did not allow players to transfer in their Pokémon from previous generations and, because of this, many older Pokémon were completely unavailable in the games until [*Pokémon FireRed* and *LeafGreen*](/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen") were released a few years later.[[131]](#cite_note-NWR-137) Meanwhile, many of the new Pokémon designs, such as those for [Torchic](/wiki/Torchic "Torchic"), [Feebas](/wiki/Feebas "Feebas"), [Luvdisc](/wiki/Luvdisc "Luvdisc"), [Castform](/wiki/Castform "Castform") and [Clamperl](/wiki/Clamperl "Clamperl"), were criticized for being unoriginal.[[5]](#cite_note-HardcoreGamer-5)[[131]](#cite_note-NWR-137)[[132]](#cite_note-138) Contrastingly, some designs, including [Breloom](/wiki/Breloom "Breloom"), [Aggron](/wiki/Aggron "Aggron"), and the aforementioned Castform were praised for their coolness, with the large variety of unique legendary Pokémon also helping the third generation feel fresh and new.[[133]](#cite_note-139) While *Ruby* and *Sapphire* were recognized for introducing less memorable designs than their predecessors, designs like [Milotic](/wiki/Milotic "Milotic"), [Salamence](/wiki/Salamence "Salamence"), [Metagross](/wiki/Metagross "Metagross"), Rayquaza, and [Blaziken](/wiki/Blaziken "Blaziken") made the overall generation a satisfying supplement to the existing Pokédex.[[134]](#cite_note-140)

The third generation has had its share of enduringly popular designs. Eighteen years after the release of *Ruby* and *Sapphire*, Rayquaza and [Gardevoir](/wiki/Gardevoir "Gardevoir") finished eighth and ninth in 2020's Pokémon of the Year vote, with [Flygon](/wiki/Flygon "Flygon"), [Sceptile](/wiki/Sceptile "Sceptile"), and Blaziken also among the top 30.[[135]](#cite_note-141)[[136]](#cite
